lessons.title: Find the Hours: Which Tasks Are Worth Handing to AI
lessons.objective: Rank your business's repeated tasks by hours and dollars, choose the three that are safest and most worthwhile to hand to AI first, and record the baseline numbers you will measure against in Lesson 7.
lessons.intro_html:
In Statistics Canada's business conditions survey for the second quarter of 2026, 19.2% of businesses said they had used AI to produce goods or deliver services in the previous 12 months. That figure cannot tell you whether AI would pay in your shop. A count of your own week can.

This course assumes you can already use an AI chat assistant and write a clear prompt; the free AI for Beginners course covers that. Each of the seven lessons adds one page to a single folder or phone note called your AI playbook. Today's page is a ranked list of your repeated tasks and four baseline numbers you will come back to in Lesson 7.

sections.heading: Start with a count, not a tool
sections.body_html:
It is easy to misjudge where the hours go until you write them down. For one ordinary week, keep a tally on paper or in a phone note. Each time a task repeats, record who did it, how many times it came up and roughly how many minutes it took.

Include the small ones: answering the same question about hours or prices, confirming appointments, chasing an unpaid invoice, writing up a quote, replying to reviews. If you cannot wait a week, estimate from memory today and correct the numbers as the week goes on. Write task names only, with no customer or staff names.

sections.heading: Turn minutes into hours and dollars
sections.body_html:
One sum runs through the whole course:

minutes × times per week ÷ 60 = hours a week
× 52 = hours a year
× what that hour costs you = dollars a year

Example only; replace every number with your own. A 15-minute task that comes up 10 times a week takes 2.5 hours a week, or 130 hours a year. At an example cost of $30 an hour, that is $3,900 a year.

Then halve it, to $1,950. AI usually shortens a task instead of removing it, someone still has to check the result, and you have not measured anything yet.

What an hour costs you. For your own time, use what you would pay someone else to do that task. For staff, the wage is only part of it. A rough Ontario example for 2026, in Canadian dollars, using a $25 wage you should replace (the province's general minimum wage has been $17.95 an hour since 1 October 2026): the employer's Canada Pension Plan contribution of 5.95% ($1.49), the employer's Employment Insurance premium of 1.4 times the 1.63% employee rate ($0.57), minimum vacation pay of 4% ($1.00; 6% after five years of employment) and a Workplace Safety and Insurance Board premium that depends on your industry class and claims record (2026 class rates run from $0.18 to $3.55 per $100 of insurable payroll; at an example $1.23, about $0.31). That is roughly $28.37 an hour before benefits or public holiday pay; this course rounds to $30 in its examples. The estimate ignores exemptions, yearly maximums and any other payroll costs that apply to you, and other provinces have their own rules, so ask your payroll provider or accountant for your real figure. This is general information, not legal, tax or payroll advice.

sections.heading: The four-question fit test
sections.body_html:
Hours alone do not make a task a good candidate. Put each one through four questions:

  1. Does it follow a pattern? The same kind of request gets the same kind of answer most of the time.
  2. Is it mostly words or sorting? Drafting, summarizing, rewording and grouping are what a chat assistant does best.
  3. Can a person check the result in under a minute? If checking takes as long as doing, there is little to gain.
  4. What does a mistake cost? A clumsy sentence in a draft is cheap. A wrong price or a skipped safety step is not.

Then sort the tasks into three piles:

  • This week: first drafts of replies, summaries and posts.
  • This month, with checks: quotes, bookkeeping tidy-up and staff documents. Worth doing, with every figure and fact re-checked by a person.
  • People only: pricing and hiring decisions, complaints, safety and anything a regulator cares about. AI may help you prepare; a person decides.

Tick any task that involves customer or staff personal details. Those details stay out of AI tools; Lesson 2 sets the written rules.

sections.heading: Draft, check, send, and what it really costs
sections.body_html:
Every later lesson follows one rule: draft, check, send. AI prepares, a named person approves, and the business stays responsible for whatever goes out. An assistant can be wrong while sounding sure, so the check is part of the task.

Count the real cost before you start: the subscription, if any; set-up time; the time someone spends checking each result; and what one mistake would cost you with a customer. If checking takes nearly as long as the time saved, move the task down a pile or cross it off.

Frequency matters too. Example only: a 20-minute task done twice a month is 8 hours a year, or $240 at $30 an hour and $120 once halved. An hour or two of set-up uses up a good share of that, so rare tasks are seldom worth it. Some gains, such as a calmer Monday, never show up in dollars; note them, but do not count them.

Today's exercise needs only the free plan of the assistant you already use. Free plans limit how much you can use them, and vendors change the limits without notice (Google's Gemini limits page is one example), so if you hit one, finish on paper.

sections.heading: Take a dated baseline before you change anything
sections.body_html:
Lesson 7 asks whether any of this paid off, and you can only answer if today's numbers are written down. Record the date and these four:

  1. Missed calls in the last seven days. On an iPhone with iOS 26 or later, open Phone, tap Calls (Recents in the Classic layout), tap the Filter button in the upper-right corner and choose Missed. In Google's Phone app on Android, the Home tab lists call history with an icon beside each missed call; other makers' phone apps differ. For a desk line or internet-phone system, ask your provider where its call log is.
  2. Time to first reply on your last ten enquiries. In your inbox, texts or direct messages, note the gap between each enquiry and your first answer.
  3. Hours a week on quotes, invoices and paperwork, taken from your tally.
  4. Unanswered reviews, counted on each review page you have.

If you have a Google Business Profile, its Performance report shows calls, website clicks and direction requests for a date range you set. The call figure counts clicks on the call button on your profile, so it shows interest, not whether anyone answered.

exercise.title: The one-page task audit (about 15 minutes, on paper or in a phone note)
steps: List ten tasks you or your staff repeat every week; if time is short, start with five and add the rest later. Write task names only, with no customer or staff names. No spreadsheet is needed.

Beside each task, write times per week and minutes each. With a phone calculator, work out hours a year (minutes x times per week / 60 x 52) and dollars a year at your own hourly cost. Then halve the dollar figure.
Mark each task's harm-if-wrong as low, medium or high, and tick any task that involves customer or staff personal details.

Type the list, or dictate it with your phone keyboard's microphone, into the free plan of the AI assistant you already use, with the 'Sort my task list' prompt below. Read the list over first to be sure it holds no names or personal details. Overrule the assistant wherever you know better. If the app says you have reached a usage limit, finish the sort on paper with the four questions.
Circle one 'this week' task, one 'this month, with checks' task and one 'people only' task.

Write today's date and your four baseline numbers: missed calls in the last seven days, time to first reply on your last ten enquiries, hours a week on quotes, invoices and paperwork, and unanswered reviews. If one takes too long to count today, write your best estimate, mark it as an estimate and correct it this week. Save this as page 1 of your AI playbook; every later lesson adds one page.

prompts.label: Tasks I may have missed
prompts.text:
I run a [type of business] in [city or region] with [number] staff. Here are the repeated weekly tasks I have listed so far: [task names only].

Suggest up to eight other routine tasks that a business like mine often repeats each week and that I may have left out. Ask me whether each one applies to me; do not assume it does. Do not estimate any times for me and do not recommend any product.

prompts.label: Sort my task list
prompts.text:
I run a [type of business] with [number] staff. Below is my list of repeated weekly tasks. Each line gives the task, times per week, minutes each, my harm-if-wrong rating (low, medium or high) and a Y if the task involves customer or staff personal details. The list contains no names or personal details.

For each task, answer these four questions in a few words: 1) Does it follow a pattern? 2) Is it mostly words or sorting? 3) Can a person check the result in under a minute? 4) What does a mistake cost?

Then put each task in one of three piles: "this week" (low-risk first drafts), "this month, with checks" (useful, but a person re-checks every figure and fact) or "people only" (pricing and hiring decisions, complaints, safety, anything a regulator cares about). Give one line of reasoning per task. If you are unsure, choose the more cautious pile and say why. Do not recommend any product or subscription.

My list:
[your tasks, one per line]

prompts.label: Challenge my numbers
prompts.text:
Here are my estimates for the same tasks, one per line: [task, times per week, minutes each, hours a year, dollars a year]. My hourly cost figure is [dollar amount] an hour.

Check my arithmetic using this formula: minutes x times per week / 60 = hours a week; x 52 = hours a year; x hourly cost = dollars a year. Show your working for each line so I can re-check it on a calculator. Then point out any estimate that looks too high or too low for a [type of business] and ask me one question about each. Do not change my numbers yourself.

prompts.label: What checking will involve
prompts.text: My first task to try is: [your 'this week' task]. Describe in two sentences what an AI first draft for this task would look like. Then list the three things a person in my business should check before the result is sent or used, and estimate the checking time in seconds. Finish with the details I should never put in the prompt, such as customer names, contact details or payment information. Keep the whole answer under 150 words.

checklist: I have listed my repeated tasks (ten, or at least five to start) with times per week and minutes each.
Each task has hours a year and a halved dollars-a-year figure, worked out with my own hourly cost.
Each task is marked low, medium or high for harm-if-wrong, and tasks involving personal details are ticked.
I have circled one 'this week' task, one 'this month, with checks' task and one 'people only' task.
Today's date and my four baseline numbers are written down.
The page is saved as page 1 of my AI playbook and has no customer or staff names on it.
lessons.takeaway: Count your week before you choose a tool: the tasks worth handing to AI first are frequent, patterned, quick for a person to check and cheap to get wrong, and a dated baseline is the only way you will know later whether it paid.

lessons.title: Set the Ground Rules: Staff AI Policy, Privacy and Approved Tools
lessons.objective: Write a one-page staff AI policy with a named privacy contact, a never-enter list and a short table of approved tools, each checked against eight privacy and cost questions.
lessons.intro_html:
Lessons 3 to 6 all have you putting business material into AI tools. Before that starts, your business needs one page of rules: which tools are approved, what never goes into them, and who checks the output.

The beginner course gave you a personal traffic-light rule for what to type. This lesson turns it into a rule for everyone who works for you, with a named privacy contact and a short table of approved tools. It becomes page 2 of your AI playbook.

sections.heading: Why the rules come before the tools
sections.body_html:
Canada's federal private-sector privacy law, PIPEDA, applies to organizations that collect, use or disclose personal information in the course of commercial activity. Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec have their own private-sector laws that generally apply instead for business inside the province, though PIPEDA still covers personal information that crosses a border. Ontario has a separate health-information law, PHIPA.

What matters for AI: the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) says a business stays responsible for personal information it transfers to a third party for processing, and must use a contract or other means to get comparable protection. An AI vendor is a third party. The usual leak is not a hack. It is a well-meaning employee pasting a customer's details into a personal free account nobody at the business chose.

Bill C-36, which would enact a new federal privacy law, was introduced on 15 June 2026. On 6 October 2026, when this lesson was checked, it was at second reading in the House of Commons and had not passed, so this lesson describes the law in force.

sections.heading: Four privacy moves for a small business
sections.body_html:
1. List what you hold. Write down the kinds of personal information you keep (contact details, addresses, payment records, appointment or health notes) and which software touches each.
  2. Name a privacy contact. PIPEDA's accountability principle requires someone to be responsible for compliance, and its openness principle expects that person's name or title and contact information to be available. Usually that is the owner.
  3. Update your notice. OPC guidelines expect you to tell customers in clear language that their information may be processed in another country and may be accessible to law enforcement and national security authorities there. Add a line to your privacy notice or intake form saying you use service providers, including AI tools, that may do this.
  4. Know the breach steps. Contain it, write down what happened, and assess whether there is a "real risk of significant harm". If there is, PIPEDA requires a report to the Privacy Commissioner and notice to the people affected as soon as feasible. Keep a record of every breach for 24 months. Knowingly ignoring these duties is an offence, with fines of up to $100,000. OPC guidance treats the business that controls the information as responsible for reporting even when the breach happens at its processor.

Staff records differ: PIPEDA covers employee information only in federally regulated businesses such as banks, so in most Ontario shops keeping staff files out of AI tools is good practice rather than a PIPEDA duty. Questions go to the OPC Information Centre at 1-800-282-1376, Monday to Friday, 9 am to 4 pm Eastern. This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: Plans and settings matter more than the brand
sections.body_html:
The same assistant can be safe or unsafe depending on the plan and its switches. From the vendors' own pages on 6 October 2026:

  • Personal plans. For the personal Gemini app, Google says a subset of chats is read by human reviewers, reviewed chats can be kept for up to three years, and users should not enter confidential information.
  • Business plans. Google says Workspace content is not used to train models outside your domain without permission. Anthropic says inputs and outputs from its commercial products, such as Claude for Work, are not used for training by default unless you send feedback or opt in (its Team plan needs at least two members). Microsoft says Copilot prompts and responses used by organizations under its commercial terms are not used to train foundation models.

So the policy says business accounts only, one login each, two-step sign-in. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's generative AI guidance recommends setting policies on how AI is used, multi-factor authentication, and keeping personal or sensitive business data out of prompts.

Choose in this order. First, AI features inside software you already pay for (email, accounting, booking, point of sale). For example, on the same day Google's Canadian pricing page listed its Workspace Standard plan at CA$18.40 per user per month on monthly billing, before tax and before introductory or annual-commitment discounts, with Gemini in Gmail, Docs and Meet. Prices change, so check the page yourself. Second, one general assistant. Specialized tools last. Cancel anything that overlaps.

Example arithmetic, replace the numbers with your own: $35 a seat x 3 staff x 12 months = $1,260 a year. At an example cost of $30 an hour, that tool must save 42 hours a year, just under 50 minutes a week across the whole team, to pay for itself.

sections.heading: Eight questions for any tool or vendor
sections.body_html:
Answer these from the vendor's own pricing and privacy pages, not from a sales call.

  1. Is our data used to train the model?
  2. Where is it stored, and who can see it?
  3. Can I add and remove staff and see usage?
  4. What is the all-in price, including overage, and in which currency?
  5. Is it month to month?
  6. Can I export everything when I leave?
  7. Is there support I can reach?
  8. Can I speak to a current customer like me?

Red flags in a pitch: guaranteed leads or rankings, no published prices, long lock-in, "set and forget" claims, a guaranteed grant, or terms under which the vendor owns your phone number, ad account or website. On grants, BDC's page says the Canada Digital Adoption Program stopped accepting new applications for its Boost Your Business Technology stream on 19 February 2024, so check any funding claim at the source.

sections.heading: The seven lines of a workable staff policy
sections.body_html:
1. Approved tools only, on business accounts, with one login each and two-step sign-in.
  2. The never-enter list, in your own plain words.
  3. A named person reviews anything before it reaches a customer or the books.
  4. Honesty: say when someone is dealing with an automated system, and no fake reviews, testimonials or results.
  5. No AI-only decisions about people.
  6. Marketing messages pass the Lesson 4 anti-spam check.
  7. Mistakes are reported fast and without blame, and here is who to tell.

Line 4 reflects the generative AI principles Canada's federal, provincial and territorial privacy commissioners published in December 2023: people should know when they are dealing with a generative AI tool.

Some readers have extra rules. Ontario clinics handle health information under PHIPA. Quebec's private-sector law, updated by Law 25, adds duties such as a privacy impact assessment before personal information is sent outside Quebec. Regulated professionals should ask their regulator before using AI with client files. Review the page every six months; tools, prices and the law change. This is general information, not legal advice.

exercise.title: Write and sign your one-page staff AI policy (about 15 minutes for the draft, of which about 10 is in your AI assistant; initials and vendor checks can finish this week)
steps: Ask every staff member, with no blame attached, which AI tools they already use for work, and add your own. List every AI or software subscription you pay for.

Pick the one or two tools you will approve. Run each through the eight questions using the vendor's own pricing and privacy pages, then mark it approved, approved with limits or not approved. If you find two subscriptions doing the same job, cancel one.

Write your never-enter list in your own plain words. For example: customer names with health or payment details, card numbers, social insurance numbers, passwords, staff records, anything told to you in confidence.

Give your AI assistant the seven lines, your approved-tools table and your never-enter list (rules only, no real customer or staff details) and ask for a one-page policy. A free AI chat app is fine for this step because nothing confidential goes in. If you wrote a one-page rule in the beginner course, start from that. Rewrite anything that does not sound like your shop.
Add the privacy contact's name and the 'if something goes wrong' step: who to tell the same day, and that this person contains it, writes down what happened and assesses the risk.

In each approved tool, set the training and history options to match the policy and turn on two-step sign-in. Lesson 6 of the beginner course covers changing the key privacy settings; if you cannot find a switch, search the vendor's own help pages.
Date the page, have each staff member read and initial it (a solo owner signs it too), and put a six-month review in your calendar. Save it as page 2 of your AI playbook.

prompts.label: Ask staff what they already use
prompts.text: Write a short, friendly message to my [number] staff at [business name]. Ask which AI tools they already use for work, whether each is on a personal or a business account, and which tasks they use it for. Make it clear nobody is in trouble and that I am asking so we can agree on approved tools and simple rules. Ask for replies by [date]. Keep it under 90 words, in a [tone] tone.

prompts.label: Check a vendor against the eight questions
prompts.text: I am deciding whether to approve [tool name and plan] for my business. Below is text I copied today from the vendor's own pricing page and privacy page: [paste the page text]. Using only that text, answer these eight questions: 1) Is our data used to train the model? 2) Where is it stored and who can see it? 3) Can I add and remove staff and see usage? 4) What is the all-in price, including overage, and in which currency? 5) Is it month to month? 6) Can I export everything when I leave? 7) Is there support I can reach? 8) Can I speak to a current customer like me? For each answer, quote the sentence you relied on. If the text does not answer a question, write 'not stated' and do not guess. Finish with a list of questions I should send the vendor.

prompts.label: Draft the one-page staff AI policy
prompts.text: Write a one-page staff AI policy for [type of business] with [number] staff in [city, province]. Use plain language a new hire can read in two minutes. Build it from these seven rules: [paste your seven lines]. Approved tools table: [tool, plan, what it may be used for, any limits]. Never-enter list: [your list]. Privacy contact: [name or job title]. If something goes wrong, tell [name] the same day. Add a line for each staff member's initials and the date, and a review date of [date six months from now]. Do not add any rule I did not give you. At the end, list anything unclear or missing as questions for me.

prompts.label: Privacy notice line, for checking before you publish
prompts.text: Draft two plain-language sentences for the privacy notice and intake form of [type of business] in [province]. They should say that we use outside service providers, including AI tools, to [purposes, for example draft replies and summarize notes], that these providers may process information outside Canada, where it may be accessible to law enforcement and national security authorities in that country, and that people can contact [privacy contact name or title] at [business email or phone] with questions. Give me two versions, one shorter than the other. This is a draft only; I will have the wording checked before I publish it.

checklist: I asked staff which AI tools they already use and listed every subscription we pay for.
Each approved tool passed the eight questions from the vendor's own pages, and any overlapping subscription is cancelled.
Approved tools are on business accounts with one login per person, two-step sign-in on, and training and history settings matched to the policy.
My never-enter list is written in my own words and every staff member has read it.
A privacy contact is named, the policy says who to tell when something goes wrong, and our privacy notice mentions service providers outside Canada.
The policy is dated and initialled, saved as page 2 of the AI playbook, with a six-month review in the calendar.
lessons.takeaway: Your business answers for customer information wherever it goes, so put the approved tools, the never-enter list and the named reviewer on one signed page before anyone uses AI on customer work.

lessons.title: Answer Customers Faster: Replies, Reviews and FAQs
lessons.objective: Build a one-page business facts sheet and use it to produce saved replies, a review response and an FAQ that are accurate enough to send after a quick check.
lessons.intro_html:
Most customer questions are the same handful asked again and again: price, hours, area, availability, how to book. This lesson turns them into replies you can send in seconds, starting with the step that stops an AI assistant from making things up about your business.

You will finish with page 3 of your AI playbook: a one-page facts sheet, five saved replies and one posted review response. The Lesson 1 rule still applies: draft, check, send.

sections.heading: Write the facts sheet first
sections.body_html:
An assistant does not know your prices, hours, service area or policies. Asked to answer a customer, it fills each gap with something plausible, and a plausible wrong price is worse than a slow reply. The fix is one page of facts it must work from.

Use these headings:

  • Hours, including holidays
  • Area served
  • Services, with starting prices or ranges
  • How to book
  • Payment methods
  • Warranty, refund and cancellation terms
  • What you do not do
  • Your tone, in three or four words

Customer personal details stay off the sheet. Each time you use it, add one standing instruction: "Use only the facts sheet. If the answer is not there, say I will check and get back to you." Then test it with questions the sheet does not cover. If the assistant guesses, tighten the wording before you trust any draft.

A phone note pasted at the top of each chat works with any assistant. Some can hold the sheet for you: when this lesson was checked on 6 October 2026, Claude's help centre said free accounts can create up to five projects, each with its own instructions and documents, and OpenAI's help centre listed projects for free ChatGPT users with up to five files each. Limits change, so check your own tool, and use the one your Lesson 2 policy approves.

sections.heading: Build the reply library from real enquiries
sections.body_html:
Do not guess which questions matter. Read your last 30 enquiries across email, text and direct messages and tally them. You will likely find a short list of questions that keep repeating. For each one, have the assistant draft a reply from the facts sheet with blanks for the name, date and price, then correct it against the sheet yourself.

Store the finished replies where you actually answer, so most customers get a reply with no AI involved:

  • Gmail: templates are switched on under Settings, See all settings, Advanced. Google's help page says they can only be turned on and used on a computer, not in the phone app.
  • iPhone: text replacement (Settings, General, Keyboard, Text Replacement) expands a short code into a full reply as you type.
  • WhatsApp Business app: quick replies are under Tools, and typing "/" in a chat brings them up.
  • Any phone: a pinned note you copy from. Other keyboards and messaging apps vary, so look in their settings for a saved-reply option.

sections.heading: Reviews: ask fairly, answer every one
sections.body_html:
Invite every customer the same way, offer nothing in return, and never write or buy a review. The Competition Bureau says anyone who writes or permits reviews that give a false or misleading impression could be liable under the Competition Act, says staff who post reviews must disclose their connection to the business, and lists giving customers incentives to leave positive reviews among the practices it calls astroturfing. The civil penalty for a first violation can reach $750,000 for an individual and $10 million for a corporation, or three times the benefit gained if that is larger. The Bureau's information centre is 1-800-348-5358 (toll-free in Canada).

Platform rules go further. Google's Maps policy bars payment, discounts or free goods or services in exchange for a review, and bars discouraging negative reviews or asking only satisfied customers. Google does let you ask with a review link or QR code. Yelp tells businesses not to ask at all.

Canada's anti-spam law requires consent before you send commercial messages by email, text or instant message, and a review request sent that way may be caught by it. Until Lesson 4 walks through consent, ask in person, on the receipt or with a QR code at the counter.

To reply on Google, open your Business Profile, choose Read reviews, then Reply. Google checks replies against its policies and posts approved ones publicly under the review.

  • Positive review: a short thank-you that picks up something the reviewer wrote. No offers.
  • Hard review: acknowledge it, give a direct way to sort it out offline, and say what you changed if you changed something.

Either way, never confirm that the reviewer is a client or patient, and add nothing about their visit, purchase or bill. Under the federal privacy law (PIPEDA), personal information may be used or disclosed only for the purpose it was collected for unless the person consents or the law requires it. Your province may have its own privacy law as well. Clinics face tighter rules: the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario's social media advice says a post may be deemed a breach of confidentiality even if only the patient could recognize themselves in it. If you are in a regulated profession, check with your own regulator first. This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: Turn the answers into an FAQ
sections.body_html:
Each saved reply is also an FAQ entry. Publish the same answers on your website so the question stops arriving. On your Google Business Profile, fill in the fields your profile offers, such as the business description, hours and, where available, services. Google's help pages say the profile's chat feature ended on 31 July 2024 and that the Q&A section is offered only for select business categories and regions, so check what your own profile shows before relying on it.

A wrong written answer is still your answer. Check every entry against the facts sheet, and when a price or policy changes, update the sheet first, then the replies and the FAQ.

sections.heading: The arithmetic and the limits
sections.body_html:
Example only. Replace every number with your own. 20 enquiries a week x 3 minutes saved per reply = 60 minutes, or 1 hour a week, which is 52 hours a year. At an example $30 an hour that is $1,560. The assumptions to replace: your weekly enquiry count, the minutes you actually save once checking time is included, and what an hour costs you.

The number to watch is time to first reply, which you recorded in Lesson 1. Measure it again on your next ten enquiries.

Some messages are written by a person from start to finish: complaints involving money or legal exposure, health or safety questions, and anything the facts sheet does not cover.

exercise.title: Facts sheet and five saved replies (about 15 minutes on a phone, plus two follow-ups this week)
steps: Write a first version of your facts sheet under the eight headings in this lesson. Short points are enough. Mark anything you are unsure of and fix it at the source later (your price list, booking page or written policy), not from memory.
Open the assistant your Lesson 2 policy approves, paste in the sheet and add the instruction: "Use only the facts sheet. If the answer is not there, say I will check and get back to you."
Paste in your five most common customer questions with names and contact details removed. Ask for a reply to each in your tone, under 90 words, with blanks for the details that change.

Ask three trick questions the sheet does not answer, such as a service you do not offer or a price that is not listed. Confirm the assistant says it will check instead of guessing. If it guesses, tighten the instruction and try again.
Correct all five drafts against the sheet, then save them where you answer customers: email templates, a text shortcut, messaging-app quick replies or a pinned note.

This week: draft a reply to one real review, critical or lukewarm if you have one, with the reviewer's name and any identifying details left out of what you paste. Check that it reveals nothing about their visit, then post it yourself.
This week: turn the five answers into an FAQ, check each entry against the sheet and publish it on your website. File the facts sheet and replies as page 3 of your AI playbook.

prompts.label: Saved replies from your facts sheet
prompts.text:
You are helping me answer customer enquiries for my [type of business] in [city or area]. Use only the facts sheet below. If an answer is not on the sheet, write "I will check and get back to you" and do not guess.

Write one reply to each question in a [three or four words describing your tone] tone, under 90 words. Wherever a detail changes from customer to customer, leave a blank marked NAME, DATE or PRICE.

FACTS SHEET:
[paste your facts sheet]

QUESTIONS (names and contact details removed):
1. [question]
2. [question]
3. [question]
4. [question]
5. [question]

prompts.label: Trick-question test
prompts.text:
Using only the facts sheet I gave you, answer these three customer questions:
1. [a question about a service you do not offer]
2. [a question about a price that is not on the sheet]
3. [a question about a date, guarantee or policy the sheet does not cover]

After each answer, tell me which line of the facts sheet you used. If no line covers the question, say so and give only the "I will check and get back to you" reply.

prompts.label: Public reply to a review
prompts.text:
Draft a public reply to the review below for my [type of business]. Keep it under 70 words in a [calm and warm] tone.

Rules: do not confirm that the reviewer is a customer, client or patient. Do not mention anything about their visit, purchase or bill beyond what they wrote themselves. No offers, no excuses and no arguing.

If the review is critical: acknowledge the concern, invite them to contact [role and business phone number or email] so we can sort it out directly, and mention [what we changed, or delete this line].
If the review is positive: thank them and pick up one thing they mentioned.

REVIEW (reviewer's name and identifying details removed):
[paste the review text]

prompts.label: FAQ from your saved replies
prompts.text:
Turn the saved replies below into a website FAQ of [5 to 8] questions and answers for my [type of business]. Use only what is in the replies and the facts sheet. Keep each answer under 60 words, in plain language with Canadian spelling. Replace every blank with wording that works for any customer, such as the price range shown on the sheet. At the end, list anything you were unsure about so I can check it.

FACTS SHEET:
[paste your facts sheet]

SAVED REPLIES:
[paste your saved replies]

checklist: My facts sheet fits on one page, holds no customer personal details, and every price and policy on it was checked at the source.
The assistant answered all three trick questions with "I will check and get back to you" instead of guessing.
Five saved replies are stored where I answer customers, each with blanks for the details that change.
Every customer is asked for a review the same way, with nothing offered in return, and nobody connected to the business posts one without disclosing the connection.
One review reply is posted, and it reveals nothing about the reviewer's visit or whether they are a customer.
I have written down which messages a person always writes: money or legal complaints, health or safety questions, and anything not on the sheet.
lessons.takeaway: An assistant held to a one-page facts sheet and checked by a named person gives fast answers you can stand behind, while one left to guess gives fast answers you will spend longer correcting.

lessons.title: Marketing Content and Ads That Stay Within the Rules
lessons.objective: Turn one real job or product into a week of posts, an email and ad variations, check every claim against your facts, and make sure your email and text marketing meets Canada's anti-spam law.
lessons.intro_html:
Lesson 3 left you with a facts sheet and checked answers. This lesson turns one real job into a week of marketing: two posts, a short email and a few ad lines. The AI multiplies what you give it. You supply the facts and do the checking.

It also covers two sets of rules that matter more once content is quick to produce: truthful advertising, and Canada's anti-spam law for email and text. You finish with content ready to post, a consent log and one number that shows whether an ad can pay for itself.

sections.heading: Start with one true thing, then make five pieces
sections.body_html:
Skip the request for "marketing ideas". Start from something true and yours: a job finished this month, a product that just arrived, a question a customer asked this week, the season. Give the AI tool your Lesson 3 facts sheet and plain notes about the job, and pair the result with your own photo of the work. Local detail and proof are the parts an AI tool cannot supply. Where they are missing, it fills the gap with generic wording or makes something up.

From that one job, ask for five pieces:

  • a post for your business listing
  • a social caption
  • a short email
  • a new FAQ entry
  • an ad angle

Two posts a week is about eight a month. Batch them in one sitting and that is one block of time, not eight separate scrambles.

Describe the job, not the customer. Names, addresses and contact details stay out of your notes and out of the AI tool.

sections.heading: Ad lines, and the number that decides whether an ad can work
sections.body_html:
Ad platforms mix and test short pieces of text, so ask for several, written to the platform's limits. Google's help page for responsive search ads lists up to 15 headlines of 30 characters and up to 4 descriptions of 90 characters (checked 6 October 2026). Ask for three angles (price, speed and trust) with a character count beside every line, and recount any line near the limit yourself, because AI tools can miscount. Then change one thing at a time, so you can tell what made the difference.

Before you spend, work out two numbers. The figures are examples only. Replace each with your own.

  • Cost per lead = ad spend ÷ leads. Example: $300 ÷ 6 enquiries = $50.
  • Break-even cost per lead = gross profit per job × close rate. Example: $400 × 1 job won from every 4 enquiries = $100. Gross profit is what the job brings in minus what it directly costs you to deliver, and close rate is the share of enquiries that turn into jobs.

In the example a lead costs $50 and the business can afford up to $100, so the ad has room. If your cost per lead sits above your break-even, better wording will not rescue the ad. Change the offer, the targeting or the landing page, or stop the ad.

sections.heading: Four questions before anything is published
sections.body_html:
Put every post, email and ad through four questions:

  1. Is it true? Check each price, date and claim against the facts sheet.
  2. Can I prove it to a customer standing in front of me?
  3. Am I allowed to say it in my trade?
  4. Does it reveal anything about a customer?

The first two are law. The Competition Act prohibits promoting a product or service with claims that are false or misleading in a material respect, and the Competition Bureau weighs the general impression as well as the literal words. Its guidance names specific traps: performance claims with no adequate and proper test done before the claim is made, a made-up "regular price" that dresses up a sale, a headline price that leaves out mandatory fees (government charges such as sales tax aside), and untrue low-stock or deadline claims. For a first violation, civil penalties are the ones Lesson 3 set out: up to $750,000 for an individual and $10 million for a corporation, or three times the benefit gained if that is larger. The Canadian Code of Advertising Standards also says every claim must be supported by competent and reliable evidence.

So strike "best" and "number one" unless you hold the proof. Publish a testimonial only with the customer's written approval and permission, and exactly as they gave it. Never show an AI-made image as your finished work or as a real customer. Platforms add their own rules: Meta says it puts an "AI info" label on ad images created or significantly edited with its generative AI features, or created or edited with third-party AI tools.

For question 3, regulated professions have stricter rules: the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario's advertising policy, for one, bars testimonials and comparisons with other practitioners. If you answer to a regulator, read its advertising rule first. For question 4, the consent principle in federal privacy law (PIPEDA) expects meaningful consent to use personal information, and consent again for a new purpose. Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec have their own private-sector privacy laws, so check which one covers you. A photo taken for the job file is not yet cleared for an ad, so ask before showing a recognizable face, name, house number or licence plate.

This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: Email and text: three anti-spam checks
sections.body_html:
Canada's anti-spam legislation (CASL) covers commercial messages sent to an electronic address, which the Act defines as an email, instant messaging, telephone or similar account. For you that means marketing emails, texts and direct messages. Each one must pass three checks. Public posts must still meet the truth rules above.

  1. Consent, with proof. Express consent means the person agreed, verbally or in writing, to receive your messages. It lasts until they withdraw it. Implied consent is time-limited: generally up to two years after a purchase and six months after an enquiry. Whoever claims consent has the onus of proving it, so keep a simple log: who, when, how.
  2. Identification. Each message names your business and gives a current mailing address plus a phone number, email address or web address, valid for at least 60 days after sending.
  3. Unsubscribe. Each message offers a clear, no-cost way to opt out, acted on within 10 business days at the latest. If your texts say "reply STOP", honour every STOP.

AI can write the message. It cannot create consent. Under the Act, a message asking for consent is itself a commercial message, so emailing strangers to ask permission does not get you around the rule. The Privacy Commissioner's e-marketing guidance says PIPEDA prohibits harvesting addresses with computer programs, with very limited exceptions, and that you stay responsible for the consent behind any list a supplier hands you. Treat bought and scraped lists as off limits. The maximum penalty per violation is $1 million for an individual and $10 million for a business.

This is general information, not legal advice. The rules have exceptions, so check the official pages linked here or ask a lawyer before you rely on one.

sections.heading: Honest limits
sections.body_html:
AI makes content cheap for everyone, your competitors included, so volume alone will not win attention. AI copy also drifts toward the same generic phrases and can get details wrong. Three habits keep it useful:

  • Check every price, date and claim against the facts sheet.
  • Read each piece aloud once. If it no longer sounds like you, rewrite it.
  • Judge marketing by enquiries and bookings, not likes.

exercise.title: One job, one week of marketing (about 15 minutes on a phone)
steps: Pick one real finished job, product or customer question from the last month.

Give the assistant approved in your Lesson 2 policy your facts sheet and a few plain notes about the job, with no customer names, addresses or contact details. Ask for a business-listing post, a social caption, a 90-word email, and three ad headlines with one description. The first prompt below does this.
Run each piece through the four-question check. Strike out any claim you could not prove to a customer standing in front of you.

Run the three anti-spam checks on the email. Write down exactly which contacts are allowed to receive it and why, and start a consent log with three headings: who, when, how. Keep the log in your own records, not in the AI tool.
Work out your break-even cost per lead from your own gross profit per job and close rate.
Schedule or post the two posts, with your own photo of the work. Check first that the photo shows no face, name, house number or licence plate you have not been given permission to show.

Finish this week: go through your whole contact list. Remove anyone whose consent you cannot account for, and invite contacts whose implied consent is still running to opt in before it runs out. Fix your message footer so it shows your business name, a mailing address, one other contact method and a working unsubscribe. Save the week's content, the consent log and your break-even number as page 4 of your AI playbook.

prompts.label: One job, five pieces
prompts.text: Use only the facts sheet and job notes below. If a detail is missing, leave a [BLANK] for me to fill in. Do not invent prices, dates, results, reviews, awards or customer details, and do not use words such as best, number one or guaranteed. Write: (1) a business-listing post under [80] words, (2) a social caption under [50] words, (3) an email of about 90 words with a subject line, (4) one FAQ question and answer, and (5) three ad headlines of 30 characters or fewer, one each for price, speed and trust, plus one description of 90 characters or fewer. Tone: [how you talk to customers]. Area served: [city or neighbourhoods]. FACTS SHEET: [paste your facts sheet]. JOB NOTES, with no customer names or addresses: [what the job was, what you did, what makes it worth showing].

prompts.label: Ad lines to the character limit
prompts.text: Write [8] search ad headlines of 30 characters or fewer and [3] descriptions of 90 characters or fewer for [service or product] in [area served]. Cover three angles (price, speed and trust) and label the angle of each line. After each line, show its character count including spaces. Use only these facts: [paste the relevant lines of your facts sheet]. No superlatives, no guarantees, and no made-up deadlines, discounts or stock levels.

prompts.label: Claim check before publishing
prompts.text: Act as a cautious reviewer. Do not rewrite anything yet. List every factual claim in the copy below in a table with three columns: the claim, where it appears in my facts sheet (or 'not found'), and what proof a customer could ask to see. Then flag any superlative, comparison with competitors, price or discount claim, urgency wording, health or safety claim, testimonial, and anything that could identify a customer. This is a first check only; I will make the final decision. COPY: [paste the post, email or ad]. FACTS SHEET: [paste your facts sheet].

prompts.label: Message footer and sign-up wording
prompts.text: Check the marketing [email or text] below against three points and tell me what is missing. Do not judge whether I have consent; I will check that against my own records. (1) Does it clearly name my business, [business name]? (2) Does it show a mailing address and at least one of a phone number, email address or web address? (3) Does it give a clear, free way to unsubscribe? Then draft a short sign-up line for my [counter card or website form] that says what people will receive ([type of messages]), who it comes from ([business name], [mailing address], [phone, email or web address]) and that they can unsubscribe at any time. MESSAGE, with no customer details: [paste your draft].

checklist: This week's posts, email and ad lines all start from one real job and my facts sheet.
Every claim has passed the four questions, and anything I could not prove is gone.
No customer can be identified in words or photos without permission, and no AI-made image is shown as real work.
My email or text names the business, shows a mailing address plus one other contact method, and has a working unsubscribe.
My consent log has started (who, when, how) and I know which contacts may receive the email, and why.
My break-even cost per lead is written down, worked out from my own numbers.
lessons.takeaway: AI can turn one true job into a week of marketing, but the facts, the proof and the consent have to come from you.

lessons.title: Paperwork: Quotes, Invoices, Books and Staff Documents
lessons.objective: Produce a clear quote from rough job notes with every figure re-checked, set up polite payment reminders, and turn one task you do from memory into a written procedure someone else can follow.
lessons.intro_html:
Paperwork sits in the "this month, with checks" pile from Lesson 1. The wording is easy work for an AI assistant; the numbers and the rules are not. Here the assistant drafts, and a calculator, your invoicing software and a named person do the rest.

You will finish with a quote template built from a real job or a one-page procedure for a task that lives only in your head, plus a tally of every correction you made. That is page 5 of your AI playbook.

sections.heading: What AI drafts, and what it must not decide
sections.body_html:
Use your approved assistant for the parts of paperwork that are language: turning rough notes into a clear scope, ordering a document sensibly, writing reminders, suggesting an expense category, and explaining a report you do not understand.

Keep four things out of its hands:

  • Arithmetic nobody re-checked. An assistant can add wrongly and sound sure. Google's own notice says Gemini may produce inaccurate information, and Anthropic tells users not to rely on Claude as their only source of truth.
  • Tax answers. Those come from your accountant or the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) business enquiries line, 1-800-959-5525.
  • Anything sent to the CRA that a person has not reviewed.
  • Decisions about people, such as who gets hired.

Your Lesson 2 never-enter list still applies: no customer names or addresses, bank details, card numbers or social insurance numbers in a chat tool.

sections.heading: A quote from rough notes, then the number check
sections.body_html:
Dictate or type what you saw on site, just as you would jot it, and add the relevant lines of your own price list. Ask for six parts: scope, inclusions, exclusions, assumptions, how long the quote is valid, and payment terms. The prices come from you. Exclusions and assumptions are the lines that prevent disputes later.

Example arithmetic, replace with your own numbers: 8 quotes a week x 15 minutes saved each = 120 minutes, or 2 hours a week.

Now the number check. Every subtotal, tax line and total comes from a calculator or your invoicing software, never from the draft. Example, replace with your own numbers and your province's rate: $1,200 plus 13 per cent HST, the Ontario rate, is $156 of tax and a total of $1,356.

Fixed details live on your template, not in the AI's draft. If you are registered for GST/HST, the CRA's chart sets out what a business customer needs on an invoice to claim the tax back: under $100, your business name, the date and the total; from $100 to $499.99, also your registration number and the GST/HST charged (or a note that it is included); at $500 or more, also the buyer's name, a brief description and the payment terms. For most businesses the CRA's small-supplier limit is $30,000 of taxable sales, counted over a single calendar quarter or the last four in a row. Once you pass it you must register; the CRA's registration page explains the timing.

Ontario: the province's consumer contract page says that when a written estimate is included in a consumer contract, the final price cannot be more than 10 per cent above it unless the customer agrees to a new price and signs a change to the contract. This is general information, not legal advice; for tax questions, ask your accountant or the CRA.

sections.heading: Getting paid, keeping books, and one fraud check
sections.body_html:
Write a firm, polite three-message reminder sequence once and reuse it: a few days before the due date, the day after, and one to two weeks late. First check what your invoicing software already sends. On 6 October 2026, for example, Wave's invoicing page listed automatic overdue reminders as a feature of its Pro plan, and QuickBooks' Canadian invoicing page described reminder emails for invoices coming due or overdue. Check each vendor's pricing page for current plans and costs.

Do not let an assistant invent late-fee wording. Under section 4 of the federal Interest Act, when a written contract states interest by the day, week or month, no more than 5 per cent a year can be charged or recovered unless the contract also states the equivalent yearly rate (mortgages are excepted). Have your accountant or lawyer settle that line before it goes on your template. This is general information, not legal advice.

For the books, AI can explain a statement, suggest categories and prepare questions for your accountant, working from descriptions and totals, never account numbers. Your bookkeeper or accountant has the final word. The CRA says to keep records and supporting documents for six years from the end of the last tax year they relate to. Scanned images of paper receipts are accepted only if the scanning meets a national standard, so keep the originals until your accountant confirms yours does. The CRA also says records kept outside Canada and reached electronically from Canada do not count as kept in Canada; ask your accountant how that affects your cloud software.

One fraud check belongs here. The Competition Bureau warns that AI can clone a voice and write messages in a specific person's style, and the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre describes spoofed emails telling a business that a supplier's payment details have changed. Before paying to new or changed bank details, phone the supplier on a number you already had, never one given in the message. Report fraud to your local police and to the Centre at 1-888-495-8501 or through its reporting page.

sections.heading: Staff documents: procedures and hiring
sections.body_html:
Small businesses hire rarely but re-explain constantly. Example arithmetic, replace with your own numbers: 20 minutes x 6 times a month = 2 hours a month, or 24 hours a year.

Record a voice note talking through one task from start to finish. Some phones can turn a recording into text; Apple's Voice Memos page explains transcripts on iPhone, so check there whether your model and region are covered. Otherwise dictate straight into the assistant. Ask for numbered steps, a check after each risky step and clear "stop and ask" points. Then let the newest person try it and note where they get stuck.

For hiring, AI can tighten a job posting and draft duty-based interview questions. The Ontario Human Rights Commission advises setting questions in advance from the job's essential duties and asking every applicant the same ones. You remove anything touching a protected ground, such as age, family status, disability or place of origin. A person makes every hiring decision and can explain it. Resumes stay out of consumer chat tools; that is the safe default, since the privacy law covering applicants varies by province and industry.

Ontario employers with 25 or more employees: since 1 January 2026, a publicly advertised job posting must show expected pay or a range no wider than $50,000 a year (not required for jobs paying more than $200,000), say if AI is used to screen, assess or select applicants, say whether it is for an existing vacancy, and carry no Canadian-experience requirement. Interviewed applicants must be told within 45 days of their last interview whether a hiring decision has been made. Elsewhere, ask your province's employment standards office.

An AI-written procedure never replaces training the law requires. In Ontario that includes basic health and safety awareness training for workers and supervisors, Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) training before workers use hazardous products, accessible customer service training for employees and volunteers, and at least one certified food handler on site during every hour a food premises operates. This is general information, not legal advice.

exercise.title: Choose your track: a checked quote or a written procedure (about 10 to 15 minutes each, on a phone)
steps: Pick the track that matches the 'this month' task you circled in Lesson 1, and plan to do the other one later this week.

Money track: take a real job you quoted recently or one waiting on your desk. Dictate or type the rough notes exactly as you would jot them, add the relevant lines of your own price list (no customer name or address), and ask your approved assistant for a quote with scope, inclusions, exclusions, assumptions, validity period and payment terms in plain language.

Money track: recalculate every figure with a calculator or your invoicing software and fix anything that differs. Save the corrected result as your quote template and add one overdue-payment reminder beside it.

People track: pick one task that lives only in your head (opening up, handling a return, booking a new client, closing the till). Record a three-minute voice note explaining it start to finish and get the transcript, or dictate straight into the assistant. Leave out customer and staff names. Ask for a one-page procedure: numbered steps, a check after any step where a mistake costs money or safety, and a 'stop and ask the owner' list.
People track: later this week, hand the procedure to a staff member or a friend, note every question they ask, and add the missing steps.
On either track, keep a tally of every correction you had to make, and write down who checks the numbers and who checks the wording.
Save the template or procedure, with the tally, as page 5 of your AI playbook. The tally comes back in Lesson 7.

prompts.label: Quote from rough notes
prompts.text:
Turn my rough site notes into a customer quote for a [type of business] in [province]. Use only my notes and my price list below. Do not invent prices, quantities or timelines. Where something is missing, write CHECK in capitals and list it at the end as a question for me. Lay it out as: scope of work, what is included, what is excluded, assumptions, how long the quote is valid ([number] days), and payment terms ([your payment terms]). Use plain language and no sales talk. Do not calculate tax or totals; leave those lines blank for me to fill in from my invoicing software.

My notes: [paste your notes, with no customer name or address]

My price list lines: [paste the relevant lines]

prompts.label: Three payment reminders
prompts.text: Write three short payment reminders for a [type of business], firm and polite, each under 80 words: one to send [number] days before the due date, one for the day after it, and one for [number] days late. Leave clearly marked blanks for the customer's first name, invoice number, amount, due date and how to pay, which I will fill in myself outside this chat. Do not mention interest, late fees or legal action. Do not add any facts I have not given you.

prompts.label: Voice note to one-page procedure
prompts.text:
Below is a transcript of me explaining how we [task] at my [type of business]. Turn it into a one-page procedure a new employee could follow on their first day: numbered steps in order, a check after any step where a mistake could cost money or affect safety, and a final list headed 'Stop and ask [owner or manager]'. Keep my wording where it is clear. Do not add steps I did not describe. Instead, list anything that seems to be missing as questions for me at the end.

Transcript: [paste the transcript, with no customer or staff names]

prompts.label: Same interview questions for every candidate
prompts.text: Draft [number] interview questions for a [job title] at a [type of business]. Tie each question to one of these duties: [list the main duties]. Every candidate will be asked the same questions in the same order. Do not include anything about age, family or marital status, health or disability, religion, citizenship, place of origin, or where the person gained their experience. After each question, note which duty it tests and what a strong answer would show.

checklist: Every subtotal, tax line and total was recalculated on a calculator or in my invoicing software, not taken from the AI draft.
My template, not the AI draft, carries my business name, GST/HST registration number and fixed terms.
No customer names, addresses, bank or card details, social insurance numbers or resumes went into a chat tool.
Any late-fee or interest line has been reviewed by my accountant or lawyer before going on the template.
New or changed bank details get a phone call to a number I already had before any payment is sent.
Someone other than me has tried the written procedure, and my correction tally is saved on page 5 of the playbook.
lessons.takeaway: Let AI handle the wording of your paperwork, and let a calculator, your software and a named person handle the numbers, the rules and every decision about people.

lessons.title: AI Receptionists and Chat Agents: Decide, Brief, Compare
lessons.objective: Decide with your own call and cost numbers whether an AI phone or chat agent is worth a trial, write the one-page brief it must follow, and compare providers on cost, control and privacy.
lessons.intro_html:
An AI receptionist answers your phone, and a chat agent answers your website or messaging inbox, when you cannot. It can pay for itself or be a monthly bill that recovers nothing; your own call log tells you which.

You will finish with page 6 of your AI playbook: the arithmetic, a one-page brief for the agent, and a written decision of no, not yet, or a 30-day trial.

sections.heading: What an agent does, and where it breaks
sections.body_html:
A phone or chat agent can answer at any hour, reply from your facts sheet, collect a name and reason for calling, book or take a message, and send you a summary.

It struggles with poor lines, upset callers, emergencies, unusual requests and anything your facts sheet does not cover. Plan now for how those calls reach a person.

sections.heading: Run the missed-call arithmetic before you shop
sections.body_html:
Start with the missed-call count from your Lesson 1 baseline. These are example numbers; replace every one with your own.

  • 6 missed calls a week × half that were real enquiries = 3
  • 3 × a close rate of 1 in 3 = 1 job a week
  • 1 job × $250 gross profit × 4.33 weeks = about $1,080 a month at stake
  • Assume an agent recovers half until you have measured: about $540
  • Less an example all-in cost of $200 a month = about $340 a month ahead

Run the same sum with 1 missed call a week: about $180 at stake, about $90 recovered, against the same $200. That business loses about $110 a month.

Price the cheaper fixes before any agent:

  • A callback habit: every missed call returned at two set times a day.
  • Voicemail-to-text: Rogers listed a Premium Voicemail-to-Text add-on at $7.00 a month on its consumer add-ons page on 6 October 2026; business plans may differ.
  • Forwarding unanswered calls to a staff phone or answering service; TELUS, for example, describes a Call Forward No Reply setting for mobiles. Ask your carrier what forwarded calls cost.
  • A booking link in your voicemail greeting and text replies.

sections.heading: Write the brief: your playbook is the script
sections.body_html:
Your playbook is the agent's script: the facts sheet and saved replies (Lesson 3), tone and offers (Lesson 4), price ranges and stop-and-ask points (Lesson 5) and the policy (Lesson 2). Thin documents produce wrong answers. The brief has five parts:

  1. Greeting. It says it is an automated assistant and, if the call is recorded, says so and why.
  2. Three jobs it may do, such as answering from the facts sheet, booking and taking messages.
  3. A never list: firm prices outside the facts sheet; medical, legal or safety advice; taking card numbers.
  4. Emergencies: “If this is an emergency, hang up and dial 9-1-1.” Clinics can add 9-8-8, the Suicide Crisis Helpline, by call or text at any hour.
  5. Hand-off: anyone who asks for a person, or is upset, gets one or a promised callback time.

Why those lines are there:

  • Recording. Federal privacy commissioner guidance on recording customer calls says to tell the caller the call is recorded and why, and to offer another way to deal with you if they object. It does not mention AI agents, so assume an agent's recordings and transcripts count.
  • Saying it is automated. No general federal rule in force requires this, as far as this lesson's checks found (bills C-34 and C-36 were still at second reading on 6 October 2026). It is recommended practice: Canada's privacy commissioners say people should know when they are dealing with a generative AI tool, and the Competition Bureau says courts look at the general impression you create.
  • Storage abroad. Federal guidance says the federal private-sector privacy law does not bar processing outside Canada, but you stay accountable and should tell customers. As Lesson 2 noted, Quebec's private-sector privacy law requires a privacy impact assessment before personal information is sent outside Quebec. Ontario clinics: read the provincial privacy commissioner's January 2026 AI scribe guidance and ask your college.
  • Cards. Card-industry guidance puts the people and systems that take spoken card details under its security standard. Keep payments with your processor.
  • Accessibility. Ontario's customer service guidance expects staff to communicate in a way that considers a customer's disability, so always offer another route.

This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: You answer for what it says: trial rules
sections.body_html:
In Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149, decided 14 February 2024, British Columbia's Civil Resolution Tribunal held the airline responsible for its website chatbot's wrong answer about bereavement fares, calling the chatbot part of the airline's website, and ordered it to pay $812.02 in damages, interest and fees. This is one small-claims decision and general information, not legal advice. The practical point stands: the agent's words are yours.

So a trial has rules:

  • 30 days, month to month, with a written monthly cost ceiling.
  • After-hours or overflow calls only at first.
  • Twenty test calls with your own hardest questions before launch.
  • Transcripts read daily at first, then weekly.
  • Every cost counted, including set-up and your review time.

sections.heading: Compare providers on ten questions
sections.body_html:
Score each provider on the eight questions from Lesson 2, plus two for phone agents: who owns the phone number and the recordings, and what happens to calls when the service is down.

The CRTC, the federal telecommunications regulator, says you can keep a landline or mobile number if the new provider does the transfer while the old service is active, but a move to or from an internet-based (VoIP) service might need a new one. Get it in writing that a vendor-supplied number can be transferred out. Ask how 9-1-1 works on any internet-based line; the CRTC requires many of those providers to explain its limits.

Two examples of pricing models, from the vendors' own pages on 6 October 2026. They are not recommendations or averages:

  • Per call: Smith.ai's AI Receptionist listed a free tier of 25 calls a month, then $3.00 a call, and a Pro plan at $150 a month for 75 calls. Month to month, with 30 days' notice to cancel. The page names no currency, so confirm it before you sign.
  • Phone plan plus call bundle: Quo listed plans from US$19 per user per month on monthly billing, each with an AI agent and 10 agent-handled calls a month; a US$25 a month tier covers 40 calls, then US$0.75 a call, with taxes and fees extra.

Neither page says plainly whether you get a Canadian local number; add it to your list to ask.

This lesson stops at inbound calls. The CRTC allows sales calls by automated calling device only with the person's prior express consent, National Do Not Call List rules also apply, and marketing texts fall under the Lesson 4 anti-spam checks. Leave outbound until you have had advice. This is general information, not legal advice.

exercise.title: The agent brief and the decision (steps 1 to 4 take about 10 minutes with your approved AI assistant; the provider scoring in step 5 and the final decision can finish this week)
steps: Run the missed-call arithmetic with your own numbers from your Lesson 1 baseline: missed calls a week, the share that were real enquiries, your close rate and your gross profit per job. Write down the monthly amount at stake and half of it as the assumed recovery. The first prompt below checks your sums.

Write one line each for what two cheaper options would cost you a month, choosing from a callback habit, voicemail-to-text, forwarding unanswered calls and a booking link. Use the price on your own carrier's page, not the example in this lesson; if you do not have it to hand, write "to check".
Write your one-page agent brief as five short headings with one or two lines each: the greeting with its disclosure, three permitted jobs, your never list, the emergency line and the hand-off rule.

Give the brief and your facts sheet (no customer names, numbers or details) to the assistant your Lesson 2 policy approves. Have it tidy the wording, then ask it to play a difficult caller against the brief. Note every place the brief breaks and add the missing line.

This week: open two providers' public pricing and privacy pages, or one provider and the cheaper option you already have, and score each on the ten questions. Anything not published goes on a list to ask in writing.

Record your decision as no, not yet, or a 30-day trial with a monthly cost ceiling, and give the reason in one sentence. Save the arithmetic, the brief, the scorecard and the decision as page 6 of your AI playbook.

prompts.label: Check my missed-call arithmetic
prompts.text:
Check my arithmetic and show every step so I can repeat it on a calculator. My numbers: [missed calls a week], [share of those that were real enquiries, as a fraction or per cent], [close rate], [gross profit per job in dollars], [all-in monthly cost of the agent in dollars, including set-up spread over 12 months and my review time].

Work out: missed calls x share x close rate x gross profit x 4.33 = monthly amount at stake. Then half of that as the assumed recovery. Then the recovery minus the monthly cost.

Finish with two lines: how many missed calls a week I would need to break even, and which of my five numbers changes the result most if I have it wrong. Do not add any industry averages or statistics.

prompts.label: Tidy my agent brief
prompts.text:
You are helping me write a one-page brief for an automated phone or chat assistant at [business name], a [type of business] in [city or area served].

My draft brief: [paste your draft]

My facts sheet: [paste your facts sheet, with no customer names or details]

Rewrite the brief in short, plain sentences under five headings: Greeting, Three jobs it may do, Never, Emergencies, Hand-off. Keep every rule I wrote. Do not add services, prices or promises that are not in the facts sheet.

The greeting must say the caller has reached an automated assistant and must say [that the call is recorded for (purpose) / that the call is not recorded]. The Emergencies line must tell the caller to hang up and dial 9-1-1. The Hand-off line must say how a caller reaches a person: [transfer to (role) / a callback within (time)].

At the end, list any gap or contradiction you found instead of filling it with a guess.

prompts.label: Play a difficult caller
prompts.text:
Act as a caller to [business name]. I will reply as the automated assistant and I may only use this brief: [paste your brief].

Run five short calls, one at a time, and wait for my reply after each thing you say. Make them hard:
1. An upset customer complaining about [a complaint you really get].
2. Someone pushing for a firm price on [a job or service that is not on the facts sheet].
3. Someone describing [an emergency in your trade or setting].
4. Someone who asks for a real person three times.
5. Someone who starts to read out a card number.

After the fifth call, list each moment where the brief gave me no clear instruction, and suggest one plain line to add to the brief for each. Use invented callers only, with no real names, phone numbers or card numbers.

prompts.label: Provider scorecard and questions to send
prompts.text:
I am comparing providers of an AI phone or chat agent for my business. Below is text I copied today from the public pricing and privacy pages of [Provider A] and [Provider B].

[paste the text from each provider's pages]

Make a table with one row for each question and one column for each provider:
1. Is our data used to train the model?
2. Where is it stored and who can see it?
3. Can I add and remove staff and see usage?
4. What is the all-in price including overage, and in which currency?
5. Is it month to month, and how much notice to cancel?
6. Can I export everything when I leave?
7. Is there support I can reach?
8. Can I speak to a current customer like me?
9. Who owns the phone number and the recordings, and can the number be transferred out?
10. What happens to calls when the service is down?

Answer only from the pasted text and quote the few words you relied on. Where the text does not answer, write "not published" and do not guess. Then draft a short, polite email to each provider asking only its unanswered questions, signed [your name and business].

checklist: My missed-call arithmetic uses my own numbers, and I priced at least two cheaper options before any agent.
My brief opens by saying the caller has reached an automated assistant and whether, and why, the call is recorded.
My never list covers prices outside the facts sheet, medical, legal or safety advice, and card numbers.
Emergencies are sent to 9-1-1, and any caller can reach a person or get a promised callback time.
Nothing I pasted into the assistant contained a customer's name, number or details.
Each provider is scored on all ten questions, with unpublished answers on a list to ask in writing.
My decision (no, not yet, or a 30-day trial with a monthly cost ceiling) is on page 6 of my playbook with a one-sentence reason.
lessons.takeaway: An AI receptionist earns a trial only when your own missed-call numbers beat its all-in cost and the cheaper fixes, and it is only as safe as the one-page brief you write for it.
